title: Navigation for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: Navigation for a recruiting firm site
excerpt: Label the site as a map of searches, not departments. Use words a hiring manager already uses, and keep one path that briefs the search.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, a single path rather than a cluster of side streets.
caption: A navigation should look like one road toward the brief. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What labels belong in a recruiting firm's main navigation?
faqs.answer: Use the kind of role, how a search runs, the fee, proof, and a brief. Those match the questions a hiring manager arrived with. Department names such as Insights or Careers can exist as quieter links. They should not be the primary row.

faqs.question: How many items should the header hold?
faqs.answer: Five is enough, and one of them should brief the search. More than that turns the bar into a hallway. Extra pages belong inside a section. Do not add a large panel of links to avoid choosing clearer words.

faqs.question: How should the menu behave on a phone?
faqs.answer: Use the same labels, in the same order, with the brief still obvious when the menu opens. Do not depend on hover. Give each item enough space to tap, and do not hide the only action under a tall image.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A recruiting firm website navigation is a map of the searches you fill, not a list of departments. A hiring manager who has been burned before should see labels they already use, and one path that briefs the search. "About, Services, Insights, Careers, Contact" is an office directory. It does not say whether you fill their seat.

W3C's WCAG 2 overview organizes the guidelines under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Labels fail the understandable principle when they are private jargon. A menu fails the operable principle when the only way through is a hover a visitor cannot reach. Nielsen Norman Group's research puts a clock on the labels: the first 10 seconds decide whether people stay, and many leave within 10 to 20 seconds. They will not open an item to learn what the word meant.

## Jobs, not departments

Name the items the way the buyer names the work. The kind of role, or the few kinds you fill. How a search runs. The fee shape. Proof, meaning a decision you can tell. A brief. That map matches the questions they arrived with. Do you fill this seat. How do you work. What does it cost. Have you made a hard choice. How do I start.

Department labels answer the staff's questions. Where the blog lives. Where candidates apply. Who sits in marketing. Those pages can exist. They should not be the primary row. A burned buyer who sees "Insights" first will assume the firm publishes instead of searching. Fix the bar before you commission another essay.

If you have two audiences, give them two quiet doors, not two equal menus. "For candidates" can be a text link. The primary path is the brief. A split header that says "I'm hiring" and "I'm looking" spends the first glance on a choice the hiring manager did not come to make. Assume they are hiring. Let the candidate link be findable without being the headline.

Keep the row short. Five items is enough. Seven is a hallway. Extra pages belong inside a section, not in the bar that appears on every page. The bar is for the decision to stay and the decision to brief. Everything else is a room they enter after that.

## Words they already use

Take the labels from intake calls, not from a brand workshop. "Plant leadership" beats "Industrial practice." "How a search runs" beats "Our methodology." "Fees" beats "Engagement models." "Brief a search" beats "Get in touch."

Test a label by saying it to someone who has hired, with no other context. If they ask what it means, it is not a label yet. Translate it before it ships. Do not ship the clever word and hope the page underneath explains it. People who leave in the first 10 seconds do not click through for a translation.

Avoid labels that could belong to any professional firm. "Solutions." "Platform." "Network." A hiring manager has clicked those and found a brochure. Your label should be falsifiable. A wrong buyer should feel that this is not their role. That feeling means the navigation is working.

The current page should be obvious without color alone. A bold label, or a page title that repeats the label, survives a visitor who does not see the hue. A tiny underline in a pale color disappears on a phone in daylight. WCAG's perceivable principle is the reminder: information cannot live only in a color difference. Say where they are in text.

## One path that briefs the search

One item is the action. It can be a button at the end of the row: "Brief a search." It should go to the same place as the button on the homepage. If the bar says "Contact" and the homepage says "Brief a search," you have two products. Pick the brief.

The path should be present on proof pages and on the fee page. A buyer who has just read a decision should not hunt the footer to act. Repeat the action. Do not invent a second action beside it. "Subscribe" and "Brief" side by side split the bar the way two buttons split a hero.

Inside the brief page, leave the navigation visible. Do not hide it to force the form. A trapped form feels like the last firm's portal. Let them leave. The ones who stay will have chosen to.

If a search offer has its own page, the link on that page can name the offer. "Brief a plant-leadership search." The global item stays broad enough for any search you actually take. Both must be honest. Neither should open a calendar that never mentions the role.

## What does not belong in the bar

Drop these unless they are truly how a buyer decides. A blog with no tie to the roles you fill. A careers link at the same weight as the brief. A client login. Social icons. A language switch you do not maintain. A search box on a thin site that returns nothing useful.

The login can live in the footer. Clients who need a portal already know it exists. A stranger who sees "Login" in the header wonders if the real site is behind a password. That is a bad first 10 seconds. Social icons in the header ask for a detour before you have shown the role. Put them in the footer if you want them at all.

Do not add a large panel of links to avoid a labeling problem. Twenty links is a second homepage, and it usually repeats the department list you were trying to leave. If you have three role families, list those three. If you have one, do not invent children to make the menu look serious.

Footer links should match the header's words. An old footer that still says "Our process" while the header says "How a search runs" reads as neglect. Neglect reads as the last firm. Pick one set of labels and use it in both places.

The order of the five items is a sentence. Role, method, fee, proof, brief. A buyer who only reads the bar should be able to reconstruct the firm. If you lead with the firm name's story and put the role third, you have rebuilt the brochure in the navigation. Put the role first, or directly after a short wordmark. The brief stays last and visually distinct, so it reads as the action rather than as another page of explanation.

## The phone menu is the real menu

Most of these buyers will open the site on a phone between meetings. The menu cannot depend on a precise hover. WCAG applies to mobile content, and the operable principle means a person can reach the items without a gesture only a mouse can do. A compact menu is fine if it opens the same five labels, in the same order, with the brief still obvious.

Put the brief in the open menu as a button. Consider a persistent brief control when the menu is closed. Do not bury the only action inside the menu and also hide it below a tall image. The role and the brief have to be available without a hunt.

Test with a thumb. Labels that wrap into two unreadable lines need shorter words, not a smaller font. "Brief a search" fits. "Start a confidential conversation with our team" does not. The short label wins. The page it opens can carry the longer promise.

Give each item enough space to tap without opening its neighbor. A row of text links with no padding fails on a train. You do not need a novel control. You need space, the same words as the desktop, and a current-page marker that is not color alone.

Open the menu and read it aloud once. If you run out of breath before the brief, the list is still a directory. Cut an item and move it inside a page. The phone is where a burned buyer will decide, often with a thumb and a meeting in ten minutes. Design that state first, then let the wide screen inherit the same words.

## A label test you can run this week

Write the proposed labels in a plain list, with no design. Show them to three people who hire. Ask where they would click to see the kind of role, where they would click to see what a search costs, and where they would click to start. If they hesitate, change the word. Do not add a tooltip.

Then walk the built menu with one job: brief a search like the last one you wish you had won. Count the taps from the homepage. If it takes more than two, the path is still a department tour. Check that the current page is marked on each template, including the fee page and a proof page.

When the labels match the work, the pictures have to match them too. A bar that says "plant leadership" above a handshake is a broken map. Read [how to choose photographs that show the role](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-recruiting-firm) before the new labels ship on top of the old imagery.

If you want the map of a site drawn around the work rather than the org chart, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The labels are part of the design, not a list added the week before launch.
